newsitem.title: GREECE: Greenpeace protests oil spill ahead of Greek trial.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace protests oil spill ahead of Greek trial.

text.p: Greenpeace activists, who face their first trial in Greece this week, banged on empty oil barrels and locked themselves in a cage outside the Merchant Marine ministry on Wednesday to protest against oil pollution.
Greenpeace said it wanted to remind the minister that while 17 members of the international environmental group go to court on Thursday for blockading the Motor Oil refinery, polluters go unpunished.

"We are here to demand a change in the ministry's policies: 441 cases of marine pollution in 1996 show that existing policies for the protection of the marine environment have failed," said Nikos Charalambidis, a Greenpeace spokesman.

The defendants could face up to five years in jail if convicted on charges of trespass and hindering a public service company, stemming from their 24-hour blockade of the Motor Oil refinery near the Corinth canal in November.

Coast guard commandos cut through chains pinning them to mooring buoys and loading cranes at the refinery's port. The activists had taken over the facility to protest over a major spill there in August.
Motor Oil, jointly owned by Saudi Aramco and the Greek Vardinoyannis family, was fined 150 million drachmas ($650,000) for the accident at its docking facilities.
An estimated 300 tonnes of crude oil was spilled as a tanker owned by Motor Oil was unloading crude oil during a thunderstorm in the middle of the night.

Greenpeace says loading at night in bad weather spells disaster and wants stricter laws against oil pollution, more prevention measures and a ban on most oil dispersants used after oil spills in Greece, which are toxic.
"After Wednesday's protest, ministry officials pledged to satisfy most of our demands," Charalambidis said. "We'll see."
He said the ministry agreed to ban most dispersants and loading in bad weather -- but not at night -- and promised to enforce three 'tanker exclusion zones' to protect Greece's sensitive marine life.

Eight of the 17 charged will appear in court in Corinth, Greenpeace said. The defendants include activists from Britain, Austria and Germany. "The foreigners didn't come because there is a strong chance the trial could be postponed," Charalambidis said.
